newsitem.title: FRANCE: French farmers meet Chirac, stick to mad cow fight.
newsitem.headline: French farmers meet Chirac, stick to mad cow fight.

text.p: French farmers unions, clamouring on Tuesday for help to weather the mad cow crisis after meeting President Jacques Chirac, renewed pleas for aid from the European Union and for a protest march later this week.
"We were, I hope, understood," Luc Guyau, head of the FNSEA farmers association, said after the latest talks with Chirac.
Demonstrations are set for Friday in Paris and in the major cattle rearing regions of France hurt by the scare over mad cow disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
Guyau said steps taken by the French government to help cope with the crisis were seen as a "downpayment if the crisis continued".
"What we're looking for now are decisions and commitments from the European Union," he said.

EU farm ministers are due to discuss compensation for cattle farmers at a meeting in Brussels on September 16-17 and French farm minister Philippe Vasseur, present at Tuesday's talks with Chirac, said he would be on the offensive in Brussels.
Christine Lambert, head of the young farmers union, said a payout of 1,000 francs for each cow bearing calves would be needed, equivalent to about half the loss per grazing animal.
It was a question of survival for breeders, she said.
Guyau said that apart from the protests, farmers were taking other steps such as issuing open invitations for consumers to visit some 3,000 farms in an effort to restore consumer confidence in beef.

Joseph Daul, president of the national beef federation, said demand for beef had slid by 15 to 20 percent since the start of the mad cow scare and would result in a surplus of 1.67 million tonnes of meat by the end of the year. A one percent increase in demand was worth 80,000 tonnes of meat, he said.
"The best way to help the cattle breeders is, above all, to eat the beef clearly identified as healthy which we can offer (the consumer)," Daul said.

Vasseur said a European Commission proposal to fund compensation by reducing aid to cereal farmers could only be a temporary solution, while Lambert of the young farmers group warned against any attempt by the Commission to use mad cow compensation as a pretext for reducing farming aid.
The union leaders' meeting with Chirac was the second in less than two weeks for representatives of France's cattle farmers.
Several farmers had been invited to the Elysee presidential palace on August 30 after a three-week walk across much of France with a small herd of cows in tow.
As their cows munched on grass near the Eiffel Tower, the farmers were given a presidential promise that Chirac would take unspecified steps to help family farms survive.
